reader.title: Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves
bases: A settlers' vigilance committee with no stated lawful authority surrounded and shot down a camp of men it accused of stealing horses and cattle, killing sixteen to eighteen of them (A11, A15, A2, A39).

Every account has a band of forty to fifty vigilantes, acting without officers, kill nearly all of a camp of accused horse thieves after demanding their surrender to 'an investigation' (A11, A1, A15); it is 'probable' rather than certain because the killing came in a gunfight that the vigilantes' side says the campers opened, and the reports are hearsay that local papers could not confirm (A33, A2).

Separate reports from Kansas City (A1, A2), Denison via a Texas freighting point (A15), Trinidad (A33) and a later stock-growers' account (A39) agree that vigilantes killed a band of sixteen to eighteen horse thieves in the neutral strip with three vigilantes dead, though all rest on the vigilantes' side or hearsay and differ on numbers and place.

summary.text: The Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves was the reported destruction, around August 31 or September 1, 1888, of a camp of sixteen to eighteen men accused of horse and cattle theft by forty to fifty armed vigilantes in the Public Land Strip, or 'No Man's Land'.
Three vigilantes were also reported killed.
Carried by wire from Kansas City, the story ran in dozens of papers as a battle in which 'no quarter was asked or given', though no paper in the region could supply particulars.
According to the dispatch datelined Paladora, horses and cattle had for some time been disappearing from settlers' pastures and picket lines in the strip.
Suspicion fell on a band of campers in the brakes of Deer creek who said they were catching wild horses, and the settlers kept a watch on their camp.
A separate Kansas City report instead traced the trouble to a gang that had stolen horses in southeastern Colorado and fled into the neutral strip, with Colorado settlers organizing to pursue them.

A Trinidad dispatch of September 4 named John Jennings as leading a party out of Boston, Colorado, after horse thieves, among them Billy Cornellius, an ex-marshal of Boston, whose flight was believed to have led the pursuers to the main camp.
In the Paladora account, forty well armed and mounted vigilantes surrounded the camp at night and sent in a committee of six to demand the men's surrender and 'submission to an investigation'.
The campers answered with a volley that wounded one man and two horses, and the vigilantes then fired down into the ravine from the surrounding peaks.

After twelve minutes, the dispatch said, all seventeen campers lay dead or dying, while the vigilantes had three men killed and nine or ten wounded; sixteen horses were retaken and returned to their owners.
A Denison correspondent of the Austin Statesman gave a different version from John Washburn of Higgins, Texas, who had it from freighters.
In it, a vigilance committee raided the camp on Friday morning, three men sent in to demand surrender were fired on and one was killed, and sixteen of the seventeen outlaws died.
Washburn said the vigilantes were led by 'an ex-desperado of Texas' and that the people meant to 'take the law into their own hands' until the country was rid of such men.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any official action appears in the coverage, and no officer is mentioned in any account.

Three weeks later the Big Horn Sentinel reprinted a Northwestern Live Stock Grower account placing the fight near Palo Duro, Armstrong county, Texas, and naming James Ahlrich as a vigilante wounded by the first volley.
It put the vigilantes' wounded at seventeen and named 'Thompson's Kid' among the dead.

The story first appeared on September 3 in two forms: a Kansas City special from Paladora with seventeen dead, and a shorter Kansas City report headed 'TWENTY-ONE DEAD' in the Wheeling Register, which only 'supposed' that the settlers' pursuit had led to the fight.

Headlines ranged from 'A BATTLE FOR BLOOD' in the Waterbury Evening Democrat and 'VIGILANTS. They Still Exist and Fight Desperados' in the Kennebec Journal to the Indianapolis Journal's 'A Band of Horse-Thieves Mercilessly Slaughtered by a Party of Vigilantes'.

Other papers were more approving: the full dispatch spoke of 'wretched outlaws' and ended with the settlers' view that a gang had been 'subdued', and the Salt Lake Herald headed the rumor 'Horsethieves Settled.'
Weekly papers through mid-September ran condensed versions in their news summaries, some placing Paladora in Colorado or in 'N. M.'
Closer to the scene, the Trinidad dispatch reported that Trinidad, Folsom and Clayton had 'no particulars, only a meagre report of a pitched battle'.
Every account came from the vigilantes' side or from hearsay, and none gave anyone's race.
The number of dead varied from sixteen in the Denison version to seventeen in the Paladora special and eighteen in the Kansas City rumor.

The place was given as the Public Land Strip, Indian Territory, in the datelined dispatch, as Colorado or New Mexico in news briefs, and as Armstrong county, Texas, in the later stock-growers' account.

accounts.label: Paladora special (Kansas City wire)
accounts.gist: Settlers who had lost stock watched a camp of supposed wild-horse catchers in the brakes of Deer creek; forty vigilantes surrounded it, a committee of six demanded surrender, the campers fired, and in twelve minutes all seventeen were killed, with three vigilantes dead.

accounts.label: Kansas City rumor
accounts.gist: A report of a battle 'last week' in No Man's Land in which fifty Colorado settlers pursuing a gang that had stolen horses in Colorado killed all eighteen thieves and lost three men; the link between pursuit and fight was 'supposed'.

accounts.label: Freighters' report via John Washburn (Denison)
accounts.gist: A vigilance committee raided the camp on Friday morning; three vigilantes sent in to demand surrender were fired on and one was killed; sixteen of seventeen outlaws died and one escaped.

accounts.label: Trinidad dispatch
accounts.gist: John Jennings's party from Boston, Colorado, chased horse thieves into the Neutral Strip and was believed to have destroyed the main camp, but Trinidad, Folsom and Clayton had only a 'meagre report' of a battle.

accounts.label: Northwestern Live Stock Grower
accounts.gist: A later account placing the fight near Palo Duro, Armstrong county, Texas, naming a wounded vigilante and one of the dead, and reporting sixteen dead and a seventeenth dying.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Kansas City special or the rumor nearly word for word, often in news-summary columns.
The full Paladora text called the dead 'wretched outlaws' and closed that 'at least one gang of outlaws has been subdued'; the Salt Lake Herald headed it 'Horsethieves Settled.'
The later stock-growers' account said the dead included noted desperadoes who 'had at last met their deserts'.
The Indianapolis Journal headed the wire story 'A Band of Horse-Thieves Mercilessly Slaughtered by a Party of Vigilantes'.

conflicts.note: All figures are hearsay; the Paladora special is the most detailed early version.
Three vigilantes killed in every version that gives a number.

The Paladora dispatch is dated Sept. 1 in one printing and Sept. 3 in another.

record_check.dossier: Public Land Strip ('I. T.' in the datelined dispatch); Colorado only in news briefs and as the home of the pursuers; a later account says Armstrong county, Texas
Paladora (also Paladora creek), Deer creek brakes; later given as near Palo Duro
probable lynching: vigilance committee killed accused horse thieves in a gunfight
16-18 unnamed men; 'Thompson's Kid' named among the dead in one later account
Settlers' vigilance committee, no officers mentioned; the Trinidad version describes a pursuit party
Briefs date the fight to the 1st; the Denison account says Friday morning

info: About August 31 to September 1, 1888: wire briefs put the fight 'on the 1st'; the Denison account says Friday morning (August 31); the Kansas City rumor says 'last week'

A camp in the brakes of Deer creek near Paladora, Public Land Strip (neutral strip, 'No Man's Land'); also given as the head waters of Paladora creek, 200 miles northwest of Denison, and as near Palo Duro, Armstrong county, Texas
Sixteen to eighteen men described as horse thieves, 'campers' and 'desperadoes'; none named except 'Thompson's Kid', named as among the dead in a later account
Accused of stealing horses and cattle from settlers' pastures and picket lines in the strip; the Kansas City rumor says the gang had stolen horses in southeastern Colorado

Vigilantes: farmers, herdsmen and settlers of the strip (A1, A11), 'Colorado settlers' (A2), a vigilance committee led by 'an ex-desperado of Texas' (A15); the Trinidad report names John Jennings's pursuit party from Boston, Colo., possibly joined by cowboys (A33)

Seventeen outlaws killed (A1, A11, A16); sixteen of seventeen killed and one escaped (A15); all eighteen killed (A2); sixteen dead and a seventeenth dying (A39). Vigilantes lost three killed and nine (A1), ten (A11), 'several' (A15) or seventeen (A39) wounded
None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
